Mia and Leo bake a cake for Mum, but Pus the cat makes a mess.
I want to bake a cake for Mum!
Yes! We need flour, eggs and sugar.
Oh no! Flour all over the kitchen!
The cake is ready. It's a bit crooked...
Thank you so much, my darlings! This is the best cake in the world!
Leo starts at a Norwegian school. Is it scary? Only at first!
Good morning, Leo! Today is your first day at school.
Hi and welcome! My name is Ingrid. What's your name?
My name is Leo. I come from Ukraine.
Hi, Leo! Do you want to sit next to me?
Super fun! Nora is my new friend!
Dad, Mia and Leo go blueberry picking in the forest — and meet a real moose!
Today we're going for a walk in the forest!
That mushroom is poisonous. Don't eat it!
There are lots of blueberries here!
Be quiet. Now we walk home calmly.
Now we're going to drink hot cocoa.
And we saw a real moose!
Mia goes shopping on her own: milk, bread and apples — and she has to count the kroner right.
Mia, can you do the shopping for me?
We need milk, bread and apples. Here are a hundred kroner.
Excuse me, where is the milk?
The milk is over there, by the bread.
Here you go, here's a hundred.
Twenty kroner change. Have a nice day!
You're so clever, Mia! Thank you so much.
It's snowing! Leo and Nora build a snowman — and then there's a snowball fight.
Come on, Nora! Let's make a snowman!
First we roll a big snowball.
And two eyes and a carrot!
Done! His name is Mr Snow.
Nora turns eight! A present, cake and the Norwegian birthday song.
Oh no! I don't have a present!
You can draw a nice picture for her.
Good idea! I'll draw a moose.
Thank you so much! I'm turning eight today.
Here's my present. I drew it myself.
A moose! So cute! It will hang in my room.
Hooray for you on your birthday!
This is the best birthday ever!
Pus the cat is missing! Mia and Dad look everywhere: under the sofa, in the garden, in a tree...
No. But his food is gone!
There he is! He's sitting in the tree!
Welcome home, Pus! Now you'll sleep in the basket.
Ruslan and Alina from Ukraine have moved to Norway and meet their neighbour Maria.
Ruslan and Alina have moved to Norway.
Yes, we live at number four.
My name is Alina, and this is Ruslan.
Nice to meet you! My name is Maria.
We come from Ukraine, from Kyiv.
Would you like to come for coffee tomorrow?
Yes, we'd love to! Thank you so much.
Alina is ill and visits Doctor Humphrey. How do you explain what hurts?
Hello, I have an appointment at ten o'clock.
Welcome! I'm Doctor Humphrey. How can I help you?
I have a sore throat, and I have a fever.
How long have you been ill?
For three days. I sleep badly at night.
Can you open your mouth and say “ah”?
Your throat is a bit red, but it isn't dangerous.
You must drink lots of water and rest for a few days.
You can take paracetamol if it hurts. Get well soon!
Thank you so much, doctor. Have a nice day!
Denys starts a new job. His colleague Humphrey shows him the office and the Norwegian packed lunch.
Good morning, Denys! Welcome to the team.
Thanks! I'm looking forward to starting.
This is Humphrey. He will help you during the first week.
Hi! I'm from Kenya, but I've lived in Norway for ten years.
Here is your desk and your computer.
You make a new password yourself.
We eat lunch together at twelve. Do you have a packed lunch?
A packed lunch? No, I forgot!
No problem. You can have one of my sandwiches.
How kind! Now I understand Norwegian culture.
Very good! My colleagues are nice.
Ruslan and Alina view an apartment: rent, deposit, pets and the contract.
Welcome! The apartment has three rooms, a kitchen and a bathroom.
How bright and nice it is! How big is it?
It's sixty-five square metres, and it has a balcony.
How much does it cost per month?
The rent is twelve thousand kroner, and electricity is not included.
That's quite expensive, but the location is good.
Do we have to pay a deposit?
Yes, three months' rent. The money is kept in a separate account.
Are pets allowed? We have a cat.
A cat is fine, as long as it is calm.
We'll take it! When can we move in?
The first of October. You'll get the keys once the contract is signed.
Denys joins his first Norwegian “dugnad” — neighbours working together. And there are waffles at the end!
On Saturday there is a community work day in the housing cooperative.
It means that the neighbours work together without getting paid.
We tidy up, paint and plant flowers.
I'm raking leaves. Can you carry the rubbish bags?
Of course! Where do they go?
To the container by the car park.
Phew, they're heavier than I thought.
When we're done, there will be waffles and coffee for everyone!
That's the best part of the dugnad.
Now I know all the neighbours. Dugnad is a nice tradition!
Alina, a nurse from Ukraine, has a job interview in Norwegian: experience, stress and questions for the employer.
Thank you for coming. Could you tell me a little about yourself?
I'm a trained nurse and have worked in a hospital in Ukraine for eight years.
Why did you apply for this position?
I want to use my experience and at the same time develop further.
How do you handle stressful situations?
I try to keep a cool head, prioritise tasks and cooperate with my colleagues.
Your Norwegian skills are impressive. How long have you been learning Norwegian?
For two years. I've passed the Norwegian test and read newspapers every day.
Do you have any questions for us?
What does a typical working day look like, and is there an opportunity for further training?
Good questions! We will get in touch with you by Friday.
I got the job! I start on Monday.
Sunday breakfast: brown cheese, milk, eggs — and a Norwegian packed lunch for school.
Would you like bread with brown cheese?
Yes, please! And a glass of milk.
I want an egg and juice.
Brown cheese is typically Norwegian. It is sweet and tasty.
Remember to make a packed lunch for school.
Hurry up, the bus leaves in ten minutes!
A day in Nora's life from morning to night — learn to tell the time: “halv ni”, “kvart over”, “kvart på”.
It's seven o'clock. You must get up.
Yes, it's a quarter past twelve.
Shall we play football at three?
Yes! Let's meet in the park.
Nora! It's a quarter to six. Dinner is ready!
It's eight o'clock. Now it's bedtime.
Denys takes the bus to his Norwegian course: buying a ticket in the app, changing buses and getting off.
Excuse me, does this bus go to the city centre?
Yes, but you have to change at the railway station.
Can I buy a ticket from you?
No, you have to buy a ticket in the app before you get on.
Just a moment… Now I've bought an adult ticket.
Great. Take a seat, we're leaving now.
Hi, Denys! Are you going to work?
No, I'm going to a Norwegian course. It starts at nine.
Here you have to get off and take the tram.
Thanks for the help! Have a nice day!
Same to you! Good luck with the course!
Ruslan celebrates Norway's national day for the first time: the children's parade, bunads, flags and lots of ice cream.
The 17th of May is Norway's national day.
Norway got its own constitution on 17 May 1814.
Look, the children's parade is coming!
All the children walk with flags and sing.
Many people are wearing a bunad today.
It is a traditional costume from a particular place in Norway.
On the 17th of May children can eat as much ice cream as they want!
I want three ice creams and a hot dog!
Maria invites Alina and Ruslan to a Norwegian Christmas Eve: pinnekjøtt, the tree, presents — and Ukrainian kutia.
Welcome! We celebrate Christmas Eve on the twenty-fourth of December.
In Ukraine we celebrate Christmas too, with twelve dishes on Christmas Eve.
Here in Norway many people eat pork ribs or pinnekjøtt.
It is salted and dried lamb. It smells strong, but tastes delicious!
I have to taste it! We brought kutia from Ukraine.
After dinner we walk around the Christmas tree and sing Christmas carols.
At home we sing koliadky, Ukrainian Christmas carols.
And then it's time to open the presents!
Yes, and he left a present for both of you.
Thank you so much! This is the nicest Christmas we have had in Norway.
Outdoor Life and the Right to Roam
A mountain hike with a tent: what the Norwegian right to roam allows, where to camp and when fires are forbidden.
In Norway everyone has the right to walk freely in nature, even on private land.
That's incredible. Isn't that called the right to roam?
Yes, but it requires you to show consideration and not leave rubbish behind.
You should leave nature the way you found it.
Can we put up the tent here by the lake?
Yes, as long as we are at least a hundred and fifty metres from the nearest house.
Remember that it is forbidden to light fires in forests and fields in summer.
So we'll use the camping stove instead?
Exactly. And cocoa in a thermos is part of every hike!
Outdoor life really is an important part of Norwegian culture.
I understand why Norwegians love being outdoors in all kinds of weather.
There is no bad weather, only bad clothes!
Mia introduces her family — and along the way shows the pronouns hun, han, vi, dere, de, oss, meg.
There are four of us in the family, and we also have Pus the cat.
This is Mum. She is a nurse.
Hi! I work at the hospital.
And this is Dad. He is a carpenter.
I build houses. Do you want to help me today?
Mia is my sister. She is nine.
And Leo is my brother. He is seven.
I am your grandmother. You visit me every Sunday.
Yes, the cat is called Pus. It is black and white.
Who are they in the photo?
That is my aunt and my uncle. They live in Bergen.
Our family is not big, but we are always together.
And that is the most important thing!
What Did You Do at the Weekend?
Monday in class: everyone talks about the weekend — and practises the past tense (var, gikk, spilte, bakte).
Good morning! What did you do at the weekend?
I was at the cabin with my family.
It was cold, but the sun was shining.
We went skiing and drank cocoa.
How nice! And you, Leo — what did you do?
I played football on Saturday. We won three–nil!
I was there too! Leo scored two goals.
And Ruslan saved the ball three times.
I helped Mum at home. We baked bread.
Alina washed the whole kitchen afterwards.
In the evening we watched a film on TV.
The film was called “The Journey to the Mountain”. It was exciting!
On Sunday we took the bus to town and bought new shoes.
They cost four hundred kroner, but they were on offer.
Well done, everyone! Did you hear the verbs? Var, gikk, spilte, bakte.
That is the past tense — something that has already happened.
Musa from the UK, who lives in Drammen with his two children, starts a Norwegian course. Teacher Morten shows him how to introduce himself.
Hi and welcome! My name is Morten. I am your teacher.
I am from the UK. I live in Drammen now.
I speak English and a little French. And now I am learning Norwegian!
Great! What do you work as?
I am an engineer. I have got a new job in Norway.
And I have two children. They go to school here.
Norwegian is difficult! How do you say “kj”?
Say “kjøkken”. It is easier than it looks!
Now let us practise numbers. Can you count to five?
One, two, three, four, five! Easy!
Good! And seven? We can also say “syv”.
Two words for the same number? Norwegian is strange!
Today is Monday. Yesterday was Sunday.
After an hour the class takes a break.
Morten, do Norwegians drink a lot of coffee?
Yes! We drink coffee all day — in the evening too.
By Thursday you must write five sentences about your family.
I can do that. I will write about my children.
How long does the course last?
The course lasts ten weeks, two evenings a week.
Great job today! See you on Thursday.
Thank you so much, Morten! Goodbye!
Musa picks up a parcel from his mum in London: the pickup code, his ID and a nice surprise.
Musa gets a message on his phone.
Hi! How can I help you?
Hi! I am here to pick up a parcel.
Do you have the pickup code?
Yes, here is the code on my phone.
Thanks. May I see some ID?
Of course. Here is my passport.
Here you go. The parcel is quite heavy!
Thank you so much! Have a nice day!
Would you like to send anything today as well?
Yes, actually! I want to send a letter to London.
A letter to England costs thirty-five kroner.
Yes, by card or with Vipps.
It is an app for paying with your phone. Everyone in Norway uses it!
Musa carries the heavy parcel home.
Phew, it is heavier than I thought!
Dad! What is in the parcel?
It is a surprise. We will open it at home.
At home, Musa opens the parcel.
Tea and biscuits from Mum in London! Now I feel at home.
Now I am making a cup of real English tea.
With milk, Dad? That is weird!
On a trip to Bergen, Musa chats about the weather with an elderly lady. For a Brit, rain is nothing new!
You are not Norwegian, are you?
No, I am from London, but now I live in Drammen.
Here in Bergen it rains almost every day.
Then I am used to it. It rains in London too!
Ha ha! Then I must buy a good raincoat.
Musa goes into a shop to buy rain clothes.
Hi! Are you looking for something?
Yes, a raincoat and good boots.
This jacket is waterproof and warm. It costs two thousand kroner.
But I will take it. I do not want to get wet every day.
A good choice! Now you are ready for Bergen.
Now it can rain all it likes! I am dry and warm!
You see? There are only bad clothes!
Would you like a cup of coffee and a skillingsbolle?
I would love to! What is a skillingsbolle?
A sweet cinnamon bun. Bergen is famous for them.
The next day the sun is shining.
Enjoy it! Tomorrow it might snow.
The next day it really does snow.
Snow in May! Now I will believe anything in Norway!
Musa has his first lunch with Norwegian colleagues: the packed lunch, brown cheese and weekend small talk.
It is half past eleven. Shall we have lunch?
Half past eleven? So early! But yes, I am hungry.
In the canteen everyone takes out their packed lunch.
I have slices of bread with brown cheese.
It is a sweet, brown cheese. You have to taste it!
Mmm, it tastes almost like caramel!
Ha ha, now you are almost Norwegian!
What did you do at the weekend, Musa?
I went skiing for the first time. I fell many times!
It is completely normal to fall at the start!
They say Norwegians are born with skis on their feet.
Then I will have to be born again!
What do people eat for lunch in England?
Often a sandwich or a hot meal. Not open sandwiches with cheese every day!
Here we bring a packed lunch almost every day. It is cheap and practical.
Maybe I will make a packed lunch tomorrow too.
The next day Musa arrives with his own packed lunch.
Look! Open sandwiches with brown cheese — and a bit of jam!
Brown cheese and jam? Now you are more Norwegian than me!
Lunch is over. Now we have to get back to work.
Thanks for the chat! See you at the meeting at one.
The meeting starts in five minutes. I need to get ready.
Good luck! You can do it.
Maria invites Musa to a mountain cabin for the weekend — no electricity, but hot chocolate, waffles and Norwegian cosiness.
This weekend we are going to a cabin. Do you want to come along?
Yes, I would love to! But what is a “hytte”?
It is a small house in the mountains. There is no electricity there.
No electricity? What about my phone?
Two more kilometres to go. Are you tired?
A little, but the view is fantastic!
Let us take a break. Would you like some hot chocolate?
Yes please! In England we drink tea, but this is good too.
At last they reach the cabin.
It is so small! Where is the toilet?
The outdoor toilet is over there.
A toilet outside in the cold?
Yes! It is part of cabin life.
Now we must fetch water from the stream and chop firewood.
This is like a training camp!
Tonight we are making waffles and playing cards.
In the evening they go outside and look at the sky.
Look! It is the northern lights!
You are lucky. You do not see that every day.
You know what? I do not miss my phone at all.
On Sunday they walk down the mountain.
Next weekend I want to go to the cabin again!
Then you will have to buy your own skis.
Skis, studded tyres, a raincoat… Norway is an expensive but fantastic country!
taken (i det hele tatt — at all)
Musa’s first week at work: the tax card, a D-number, a bank account and his first salary in Norway.
Welcome to the job, Musa! Have you ordered a tax card?
A tax card? No, what is that?
Without a tax card we have to deduct fifty per cent tax from your salary.
Fifty per cent? That is far too much!
You order it online from the Tax Administration. You need a national ID number or a D-number.
I have a D-number. I got it when I came to Norway.
I have to log in with BankID. What is that?
It is an electronic ID. You get it from the bank.
Musa goes to the bank to open an account.
Welcome! Do you have a passport and a D-number?
In a week you will get a bank card and BankID.
A week? In England it takes one day!
Here they ask how much I earn this year. I am not quite sure.
Write what you think. You can always change it later.
Also remember to check your tax return every spring.
Tax return? Yet another new word!
There you see how much tax you have paid. Maybe you will get money back!
Your salary comes on the twentieth of every month, straight into your account.
Do I need a Norwegian bank account?
My first salary in Norway! Now I can finally buy a good raincoat.
Musa goes straight to the sports shop.
One raincoat — and new tyres for my bike!
Again? You were here last month!
Alina drops Mia off at kindergarten: rain clothes, a little cold and when to pick her up.
It is Monday morning. Alina takes Mia to kindergarten.
Have you got your backpack, Mia?
Good morning, Mia! How nice to see you!
Yes, but first you must put on your rain clothes. It is raining today.
The rain clothes are in the backpack.
Today we are going to make a campfire and grill sausages in the forest.
You make campfires with such small children?
Yes, safely and with adults. The children learn a lot outdoors in nature.
Mia has a bit of a cold. Can she be outside today?
Yes, that is fine. If she gets a fever, we will call you.
When do I have to pick her up?
The kindergarten closes at five, but many pick up at four.
Remember we have a parents’ meeting on Thursday.
Thanks! What will we talk about?
About trips, food and the new year.
Is Mia missing anything in her cubby?
Yes, extra socks, a sweater and a hat.
At four o’clock Alina comes back.
Mum! I have been outside all day!
You are completely dirty! But you look so happy.
We grilled sausages and saw a moose in the forest!
A moose? What an adventure! Now let us go home and have dinner.
Musa loves fast cars, so he buys a sporty electric one. His two daughters shout “faster!”, but Norway has strict speed limits — so the real racing happens on the track.
Musa lives in Drammen with his two daughters.
Look, kids! I have bought a new car!
Wow! It is red and super cool!
Yes, like most new cars in Norway. It goes from zero to a hundred in four seconds!
No, the speed limit here is eighty. In Norway fines are very expensive.
Many thousands of kroner! And you can lose your driving licence.
Suddenly Musa sees a speed camera.
Oops, a speed camera! Good thing I am driving slowly.
Dad, why are there so many tunnels in Norway?
Because there are so many mountains! Norway has over a thousand tunnels.
Now we need to charge the car. The battery is at twenty per cent.
About twenty minutes. Let us buy ice cream while we wait!
On Saturday they drive to a race track outside town.
Here on the track I can drive as fast as I like!
A hundred and eighty kilometres an hour! Wow!
Well driven, Musa! But remember to brake in the bends!
Dad is the fastest in the world!
And the best driver in the world — on the road I always follow the rules!
On the way home Musa drives calmly and carefully.
Dad, you are driving like Grandma now!
Yes — on the road I am a calm dad!
Musa cycles everywhere — even at minus ten degrees. He changes his tyres every month, and the neighbours call him “the bike maniac from Drammen”.
Musa cycles everywhere — to work, to the shop and to school.
Cars are fun, but bikes are the best!
Did you cycle here today too? It is minus ten degrees!
Of course! I am not afraid of the cold.
Oh no! A flat tyre again!
Dad, that is the third time this month!
No problem. I have tools in my backpack.
Yes! Hold the bike while I take the wheel off.
Hmm, the tyre is completely ruined. We need to go to the bike shop.
Hi again, Musa! Do you need new tyres?
Yes, as usual. I change my tyres every month.
In winter I recommend studded tyres. Then you will not slip on the ice.
Perfect! Then I can cycle even faster.
You also need lights and reflectors. It is dark in winter.
I have three lamps and a yellow hi-vis vest!
That will be twelve hundred kroner altogether.
Of course! Thanks, and have a good ride!
Snow, ice and darkness — nothing stops me!
The neighbours call him “the bike maniac from Drammen”.
How was the bike ride today?
Fantastic! I rode past three cars in the queue.
In spring there is a bike race in Drammen.
I am going to win! I have new tyres — again!
Nora cannot decide: is “I think” synes or tror? Musa explains it simply: synes is my opinion about something I know, tror is a guess about something I do not know yet.
Musa, I do not understand. Synes or tror?
It is easy. Synes is my opinion. Tror is my guess.
I have tasted the cake. I think it is good.
So synes is about something you know?
Exactly. I know how it tastes.
I have not tasted the soup. I think (guess) it is good.
Aha! Tror is when you do not know for sure.
I think this book is funny. I have read it twice.
And I think the new book is funny too.
You have not read it, so you guess. Correct!
Do you think it will be sunny tomorrow?
I think so. But I do not know for sure.
I think the apples here are cheap.
Thank you! I think we will get new apples tomorrow.
Remember: synes about something I know, tror about something I do not know.
And “jeg tror på deg” means I believe in you!
Now I understand! I think Norwegian is fun.
And I think you will become very good!
to think, to guess; to believe
to know, to be familiar with
Everything is mixed up at school: whose backpack, whose book and whose shoes? Leo and Mia learn to say “my” and “your” in Norwegian — the form depends on the gender and number of the thing.
No, this is my backpack. Your backpack is blue.
En sekk is masculine. That is why we say min sekk.
And does sekken min mean the same?
Yes! Both are correct. Sekken min is the most common.
Ei bok is feminine. So it is boka mi!
Quite right. Mi bok or boka mi.
Et pennal is neuter. Then we say mitt pennal.
And your pencil case is on your desk.
Where are my shoes? I only have one shoe!
Many things = mine. Your shoes are by the door.
Is this your cup or my cup?
It is my cup. Your cup is red!
Remember: min, mi, mitt, mine. And you: din, di, ditt, dine.
It is like a little song!
Now I know it: sekken min, boka mi, pennalet mitt!
And my shoes are by the door!

Musa took a bike — his own or the neighbour’s? One word changes everything: sin means “his own”, hans means “his” (someone else’s). The family sorts out hans, hennes, vår and deres with simple examples.
Musa takes his own bike. Or is he taking my bike?
Easy! I am taking my own bike — that is sykkelen sin.
The rule is simple. Sin points to the one who is doing something.
Nora leser boka si. Is that my own book?
But “Nora leser boka hans” means another person’s book.
Hans belongs to the boy, and hennes to the girl?
Leo throws his own ball. Nora throws his ball.
Two balls, two words. Now I see the difference!
This is our house, and the garden is ours.
And our books are on the shelf!
No, it is their pencil case — the children in class 2B.
Musa washes his own car. I wash his car too!
Thanks, neighbour! You are the best.
Sin is one’s own, hans and hennes belong to someone else.
And vår is ours — our whole family!
Maria has a sore throat and goes to the pharmacy. The pharmacist asks about her symptoms, suggests tablets and explains how to take them — and whether a prescription is needed.
Maria has a sore throat and goes to the pharmacy.
Hello! How can I help you?
I have a sore throat and a slight fever.
Do you have a cough or a headache as well?
A little cough, but no headache.
Then I suggest these tablets and lozenges for a sore throat.
No, you can get these without a prescription.
How often should I take them?
One tablet three times a day, after food.
Drink plenty of water and rest. Are you allergic to anything?
That will be 149 kroner. Are you paying by card?
Yes, please. And if I do not get better?
Then you should book an appointment with your GP.
Thank you very much for your help. Goodbye!
painful (ha vondt i — to have pain in)

Once a year every employee in Norway has a talk with their manager: what went well, what is hard and where to go next. Denys prepares, talks about his workload and courses — and carefully raises the question of salary.
Once a year every employee has an appraisal talk with their manager.
Welcome, Denys. Have a seat. How has the year been for you?
Mostly good. I have learned a lot, especially after I took over the project.
We have noticed that. The clients are very pleased.
Is there anything demanding in your everyday work?
I feel that the workload has increased quite a lot this autumn.
I manage the tasks, but I often have to work overtime on Fridays.
Thank you for speaking up. Then we should distribute the tasks differently.
What would you like to develop further?
I would like to take a course in project management, and lead a team in time.
I support that. We have a budget for courses in the spring.
Can we also talk about salary? My responsibility has grown.
It is perfectly fine to raise that. Salary is decided in the annual negotiation in May.
I will write down three goals for next year. Do you agree with them?
Yes, but I would like feedback every quarter.
Agreed. That will be a good routine for both of us.
Thank you for an open and useful conversation, Denys.
Thank you too. Now I know what to work towards.
sight (på sikt — in the long run)
Ruslan has lost his job and visits NAV for the first time. The adviser explains how to apply, which documents are needed and how long the decision takes.
Ruslan lost his job last month. Today he is at NAV.
Welcome. How can I help you today?
The company had to cut costs, so I was made redundant.
I am sorry to hear that. Then you can apply for unemployment benefit.
The notice, your employment contract and the last three payslips.
I have all of that at home.
You apply online with BankID. It takes about twenty minutes.
And how long do I have to wait for an answer?
Usually three to four weeks. You get a decision in your inbox.
Do I have to do anything while I wait?
Yes, you must send a report card every fortnight and look for work actively.
Thank you. Now I understand what to do.
Just get in touch if anything is unclear. Good luck!
Alina is looking for a flat and comes to a viewing. She asks about bills, the deposit and house rules — and learns that a lease can be for a fixed period.
Hi, welcome to the viewing! The flat is fifty-five square metres.
It seems bright and cosy. When is it available?
From the first of November. The rent is twelve thousand a month.
Internet is included, electricity comes on top.
Three months’ rent in a separate deposit account.
Is the contract for a fixed period or open-ended?
Open-ended, with three months’ notice for both parties.
Is it allowed to have a cat here?
Yes, but the house rules require quiet after eleven o’clock.
I am very interested. What is the next step?
Send me an email tonight, and I will send the contract tomorrow.
Musa goes to a parents’ meeting for the first time. The teacher talks about the class, a school trip and phone rules, and the parents agree who does what.
Welcome to the parents’ meeting! Nice that so many could come.
Thank you. It is my first time.
The class works well and the pupils get on together.
This term we mostly work on reading and cooperation.
I am wondering about the phone rules. Do the pupils bring phones?
The phones stay in a box during school hours. It works well.
In May the class goes on a trip. We need two adults to come along.
I can come if it is on a Friday.
Great. You will get a letter with times and a packing list.
How do I let you know if my son is ill?
Report it in the school app before eight o’clock.
Thank you for coming. Get in touch any time.
Now I feel much more confident. Thanks!
Denys has toothache. The dentist finds a cavity, explains the treatment and the price, and reminds him that dental care is free for children under eighteen.
Good afternoon, Denys. What is the problem today?
I have had a toothache for over a week.
Does it hurt when you drink something cold?
Yes, and when I chew on the left side.
I will take an X-ray … There is a small cavity here.
Does the tooth have to be pulled out?
Not at all. We will drill and put in a filling today.
You get an anaesthetic first, so you will only feel a little pressure.
How much does the treatment cost?
About a thousand kroner. Adults pay for the dentist themselves.
But children under eighteen get free treatment.
All done! Remember to brush twice a day and use dental floss.
Thank you. Then I will book a check-up in six months.
First day at a new job
Alina starts a new job. Her manager shows her the workplace and explains safety rules, lunch and how to ask for time off.
Welcome to us, Alina! Good to have you on the team.
Thank you! I am looking forward to getting started.
Here is your desk, your key card and the password for the computer.
Should I change the password right away?
Let us go through safety: emergency exit, first aid and protective gear.
Who do I report to if something happens?
To me or to our safety representative, Kari.
Lunch is at eleven. Most people bring a packed lunch.
Nice. Is it normal to eat together?
Yes, everyone sits in the canteen for half an hour.
How do I ask for time off if my child gets ill?
Then you use self-certification or carer’s days. Send a message before eight.
Ask about anything you wonder about. Nobody expects you to know everything today.
Thanks, that makes it much easier.
Nora wants to borrow books and discovers that a Norwegian library is also free courses, a language café and a place to work.
Hi! I would like to borrow books. What do I need?
Just ID. The library card is free.
Here is your card. The loan period is four weeks.
Can I extend it if I do not finish?
Yes, twice — in the app or here at the desk.
What happens if I return it late?
You get a reminder. Children pay no fee at all.
On Wednesdays we have a language café. You can practise Norwegian for free.
That is exactly what I needed!
Can I sit and work here too?
Yes, we have a reading room, wireless internet and group rooms you can book.
Then I will take these three books and come back on Wednesday.
Snow makes the bus twenty minutes late. The driver explains the connection, and Maria learns about the taxi refund rule.
It is snowing and the bus is stuck in traffic.
Excuse me, how delayed are we?
About twenty minutes. The road is slippery today.
Then I will not catch my train at ten.
There is a train twenty minutes later. Check the app.
Right, I can see it. Do I have to buy a new ticket?
No, the ticket is valid all day on this route.
And what if I had had to take a taxi?
Then you can claim a refund if the delay is more than twenty minutes.
Maria gets off and finds the platform.
Luckily I have plenty of time now.
Thanks for your help! Have a nice day.
Same to you. Take care out there!
way (i like måte — same to you)
Making a complaint about a product
Ruslan’s headphones broke after two months. He learns what a formal complaint is, why the receipt matters and that the right lasts two years.
Hello. I bought these headphones two months ago.
What is the problem with them?
The left side has stopped working, and I have used them normally.
Then you have the right to complain. Do you have the receipt?
I have it in the app. Is that enough?
Yes, a digital receipt is just as good.
We will send them for repair. It takes about two weeks.
Could I get my money back instead?
If the same fault happens again, you are entitled to that.
How long does the right to complain last?
Two years on ordinary goods, five on things meant to last.
You will get a text when they are back in the shop.
claim (ha krav på — be entitled to)
Alina is preparing for the Norwegian exam. The teacher explains the four parts, how to register and what to do if you get nervous in the speaking test.
I want to take the Norwegian exam in spring. Where do I begin?
First you register online, at the latest six weeks before.
The exam has four parts: listening, reading, writing and speaking.
Are all the parts on the same day?
No, the speaking test is usually on another day.
I am most afraid of the speaking test. I get so nervous.
Remember that you can ask them to repeat: “Kan du si det en gang til?”
And if I do not know a word?
Explain it in other words. That counts as good communication.
Which level do I need in order to study further?
Usually B2 for university and B1 for many jobs.
You already have a good vocabulary. Just keep speaking every day.
Thank you! Then I will register tonight.
Leo wants to join a gym. The instructor explains membership types, the binding period, group classes — and how to cancel properly.
Hi! I would like to become a member. What does it cost?
Four hundred a month without a binding period, or three hundred with one year.
What does a binding period actually mean?
That you cannot cancel before the year is over, even if you stop training.
Yes, all classes: yoga, spinning and strength. You book in the app.
I have never trained with weights before. Do I get help?
You get a free introduction with an instructor in the first week.
And what if I move to another town?
Then you cancel in writing with one month’s notice. Keep the confirmation.
Then I will take the membership without a binding period first.
Smart choice. Welcome — see you at training!
A neighbour explains the sorting system to Maria: blue bags for plastic, green for food waste, bottles with a deposit and a trip to the recycling station.
Excuse me, which bag do I use for plastic?
A blue bag for plastic and a green bag for food waste.
Residual waste in an ordinary bag. Cardboard and paper in a separate container.
Bottles and cans have a deposit. You get money back in the shop.
So the machine prints a receipt?
Yes, and you can choose to give the money to charity.
Where do I throw old paint and electronics?
At the recycling station. Hazardous waste must never go in ordinary rubbish.
What happens if you sort it wrong?
The refuse service may leave the bag, and the housing co-op gets a fee.
Now I understand the system. Thanks for the help, neighbour!
You are welcome. It quickly becomes a habit.
to stand (la stå igjen — to leave)
Nora books a haircut. She learns how to describe what she wants, asks about the price and finds out that tips are not expected in Norway.
Hi! Do you have a free slot today?
We have a cancellation at two. Does that suit you?
What kind of cut are you thinking of?
Just a bit shorter, about three centimetres, and some layers.
No thanks, I will leave it. But maybe some colour later.
How much are a cut and a wash?
Six hundred kroner. Colour comes on top.
It is not usual here. The price is the price.
All done! Would you like to book again in three months?
Yes please, the same day and time if possible.
Musa comes for the annual check, but the mechanic hears a strange noise in the brakes. They discuss the estimate, the guarantee and a courtesy car.
Hi! I have an appointment for the annual check at nine.
Perfect. Put the car in bay two and we will take it in now.
The brakes make a strange noise. Have you noticed it?
Yes, especially in the morning when it is cold.
The brake pads are worn. I will send you an estimate by text.
Please do. I do not want any work without agreeing first.
How long is the guarantee on the work?
Two years on parts and labour. It is all on the invoice.
I have to pick up the children at four. Will you manage?
Yes. And if you need a courtesy car, we have one free today.
The car has passed, and the brakes are like new.
Thank you very much for the quick help!
A family plans a week in a cabin. Dad checks the forecast and the avalanche warning, and the children make a packing list and learn the mountain code.
We are going to the cabin for the winter holiday. Seven days in the mountains!
Finally! Can we bring the sledge?
The forecast promises minus ten and strong wind on Friday.
Then we should go hiking on Thursday instead.
And the avalanche warning is level three. We will stay away from steep slopes.
Considerable danger. We only go on marked trails.
Packing list: wool innermost, windproof outermost, hat and mittens.
Remember the mountain code: tell someone where you go, and turn back in time.
“There is no shame in turning back,” grandma always says.
In the evening the family sits by the fireplace with hot cocoa.
This is the best holiday ever!
A difficult talk with a neighbour
Denys cannot sleep because of late-night music. He learns to raise the issue calmly: describe the fact, say how it feels and suggest a solution.
It is half past one at night and the music is thumping through the wall.
I have to say something, but I do not want to argue.
Hi! Do you have two minutes? I would like to talk about something.
Last night you played music until almost two. I hardly slept.
Oh. I did not think it carried through the wall like that.
I understand that you were celebrating. Can we agree on quiet after eleven on weekdays?
That is absolutely fine. I will tell the others too.
And tell me straight away next time — you do not have to wait.
Thanks. It is easier when we talk to each other.
We have a communal work day on Saturday. Will you join? I will bring coffee.
The residents decide whether to install EV chargers. Musa learns how a formal meeting works: make a proposal, argue for it and vote.
Welcome to the house meeting. We follow the agenda and have four items tonight.
How do I ask for the floor?
Raise your hand, and you get the floor in turn.
I propose that we install two charging points in the garage.
Good proposal. Can you justify it briefly?
More and more people buy EVs, and shared charging is cheaper than individual installations.
But who pays? I do not have a car at all.
A fair point. That is why I suggest that users pay per kilowatt-hour.
Then I am in favour. Is the investment taken from the maintenance fund?
Then we vote. Fourteen in favour, three against, no abstentions. The proposal is adopted.
Will it be entered in the minutes?
Yes, the minutes go out within a week, and the board will collect quotes.
Great. So my first house meeting was easier than I expected.
whole (i det hele tatt — at all)
Alina writes a job application and Maria shows how to make it convincing: concrete examples instead of vague phrases, and a one-page CV.
I have written the application three times, but it feels dull.
Let me read it. Often the problem is that the text is too general.
Here it says “I am structured and motivated”. Everyone writes that.
Show it with an example: what did you do, and what was the result?
I introduced a new routine that cut the waiting time by twenty per cent.
Exactly like that. It is concrete, and you can talk about it in the interview.
The CV should be one page: education, experience and languages.
Should I include a photo and date of birth?
Not necessary in Norway. For references write “available on request”.
And what if I do not meet all the requirements in the advert?
Apply anyway. Write what you can learn quickly and be honest about the rest.
Send the application today. Better still, ring the contact person first and ask one question.
Then they will remember me. Thanks for the help!
Denys gets his tax settlement and owes money. A colleague explains how to check the return, which deductions exist and how to change the tax card.
I have received my tax settlement, and I owe nine thousand kroner.
That is underpaid tax. Did you check your tax return in the spring?
I submitted it without changing anything. Was that a mistake?
Not a mistake, but the figures are only a proposal. You are responsible for them yourself.
Which deductions could I have claimed?
Travel allowance, union fees and interest on loans are the most common.
Can I appeal now that the settlement is done?
Yes, you can amend the return three years back and get the money refunded.
And change your tax card now, so your employer withholds the right amount each month.
Better than getting an unpleasant surprise next year.
You can split the underpaid tax into two instalments if you like.
Then I will. Now I understand the system much better.
Musa and Maria want to buy a flat. The bank adviser works out how much they can borrow and explains fixed versus floating interest.
Welcome. You want to apply for a mortgage certificate, is that right?
Yes, we are considering buying a flat in the spring.
How much do you have as your own capital?
About eight hundred thousand. Is that enough?
The requirement is fifteen per cent of the price, so it covers a home of around five million.
What will the monthly cost be?
At today’s rate about twenty-two thousand, plus shared costs.
Should we choose a fixed or a floating rate?
A fixed rate gives predictability, a floating one is often cheaper over time. It is a trade-off.
What happens if the interest rate rises sharply?
We stress-test your finances with five per cent higher interest before approving the loan.
You will get an answer within two working days, and the certificate lasts three months.
Perfect. Then we will start going to viewings.
A pipe bursts in Nora’s flat. She reports it to the insurer, learns about the excess, waits for the assessor and sees why photos matter.
A pipe burst during the night, and the bathroom floor was under water.
First I turn off the main tap, then I call the insurance company.
Thank you for reporting it quickly. Have you taken photos of the damage?
Yes, both of the room and of the pipe that burst.
How much do I have to pay myself?
The excess is four thousand. The insurance covers the rest if the damage was sudden.
And if the pipe was old and badly maintained?
Then the compensation may be reduced. The assessor decides on the cause.
I am drying the walls now. Do not throw anything away before the assessment is finished.
Understood. I will keep all receipts as well.
The case is registered. You get the payout once the contractor has sent the invoice.
Thank you. That went much better than I feared.
At a meeting the team argues about remote work: productivity versus community. They practise giving arguments and find a compromise.
Today’s item is how many days we should work from home. What do you think?
I get far more done at home. Nobody interrupts me every fifteen minutes.
On the other hand, we lose the small conversations that build trust.
That is a fair point, but we can solve it with fixed days together.
New employees also need someone to ask. That is harder over a screen.
Agreed. Perhaps they should be in the office more during the first months.
Let us sum up: two fixed days together, the rest is up to each person.
That seems like a reasonable compromise.
Can we evaluate the arrangement in three months?
Yes, then we will measure both results and wellbeing before we decide anything permanent.
Thank you for a factual discussion. Everyone got to say what they thought.
And we agreed without arguing. That is rare at meetings!
side (på den andre siden — on the other hand)
Ruslan has back pain. The doctor suggests a graded sick note, and his manager makes a return-to-work plan — without pressure, but with clear agreements.
Your back needs rest, but a full sick note is not always the best option.
What do you mean by that?
A graded sick note: you work fifty per cent and build your back up gradually.
Is that allowed even if I cannot lift heavy things?
Yes, the employer must adapt your tasks. I will write which duties you should avoid.
That makes it easier to talk to my boss.
Thanks for telling me early. We will make a follow-up plan together.
I can take customer calls and training, but not the warehouse.
We will write it down and have a talk every fortnight.
And if my back gets worse again?
Then we adjust the plan. Health comes first.
I was afraid of losing my job, but this feels safe.
Nobody loses their job for being ill. We find solutions.
Musa and Maria are expecting a baby and plan the leave: the father’s quota, the shared period and the choice between 80 and 100 per cent pay.
We have to apply for parental benefit before the leave starts.
How long can we be at home in total?
Forty-nine weeks at full pay, or fifty-nine weeks at eighty per cent.
The total amount is roughly the same, right?
Yes, but a longer period at home means a lower monthly income.
Then we choose a hundred per cent and shorter leave.
How many weeks are reserved for me?
Fifteen weeks are the father’s quota. They cannot be transferred to me.
I want to take leave from March. How much notice do you need?
At least twelve weeks. Then we have time to find a stand-in.
So everything is ready: the application is sent and work has been notified.
Now I am just looking forward to being at home with the baby.
The class debates whether the school canteen should drop meat. The pupils learn to build an argument: claim, evidence, counter-argument and conclusion.
Today’s claim: the canteen should serve vegetarian food three days a week.
I am in favour, and I have figures to back it up.
Meat production accounts for a large share of greenhouse gas emissions.
But many pupils already eat little protein. What about them?
A good counter-argument. Beans, lentils and eggs cover the need just as well.
Then I am willing to try, if the food tastes good.
Remember to distinguish between facts and opinions when you argue.
The figures are facts, but “it tastes better” is an opinion.
Could we propose two days first and evaluate by Christmas?
That is a sensible compromise. I will put it in our statement.
You listened to each other and changed your position along the way. That is a good debate.
I thought a debate meant winning. Now I see it differently.
The December bill was a shock. A neighbour explains spot prices, the state support scheme and simple ways to use less.
The electricity bill for December is twice as high as last year.
Do you have a spot price or a fixed price in your contract?
Spot price. I thought it was always the cheapest.
Over time it often is, but in cold weeks it swings a lot.
Yes, the state covers a share when the average price exceeds a limit. It appears automatically on the bill.
What can I do myself to use less?
Lower the temperature at night, do the laundry in the evening and seal the draught around the windows.
Is it worth switching to a fixed price now?
It is a bet. A fixed price gives peace of mind, but you pay for the predictability.
I will start with the saving measures and follow the prices for a month.
Wise. Small habits often make the biggest difference.
Ruslan does not understand why colleagues say “maybe” instead of “no”, or why everyone uses the boss’s first name. Maria explains Norwegian work culture.
I asked the boss about holiday and he said “we will see”. Does that mean no?
Not necessarily. It often means he has to check the staffing first.
Back home the boss would have answered yes or no straight away.
Here decisions are often collective. People want to anchor them in the team.
And why does everyone use the manager’s first name? It feels impolite to me.
The hierarchy is flat. Using first names means equality, not a lack of respect.
But in meetings people say little. Do they disagree without saying so?
Some do. That is why it is wise to ask directly: “Hva tenker du om dette?”
And the small talk at lunch? I never know what to say.
Weather and weekend plans are always safe. Nobody expects deep conversations.
Thanks. Now I read “we will see” as “I will check”, not as a refusal.
Exactly. And ask again in two days — that is completely normal.
Alina presents to the department for the first time. A colleague helps her cut the slides, prepare an opening and answer tough questions calmly.
I have made twenty-four slides for a fifteen-minute talk.
That is far too many. Reckon one slide per two minutes.
Start with the main message. What should people remember afterwards?
That the new routine saves us two hours a week.
Perfect. Say that in the first sentence and use the rest to show how.
And linking words between the parts: “firstly”, “next”, “finally”.
What if someone asks a question I cannot answer?
Then you say so honestly and promise to come back with the answer. It does not weaken you.
In short: the routine saves us two hours a week and it is easy to introduce.
Clear and concrete. Have you thought about what it costs to introduce?
A good question — I will check the figures and send them tomorrow.
That is how it is done. You were calm the whole way.
A letter to the local paper
Maria wants to write about a dangerous crossing near the school. The editor explains how to make the text strong: facts, a solution and no personal attacks.
I have written a letter to the editor about the crossing near the school.
Good. What is your main point, in one sentence?
That the municipality must install lights and speed bumps before an accident happens.
Then that sentence should be right at the top, not at the end.
Do you have concrete figures? Number of cars, speed measurements, near misses?
Yes, the parents’ group counted cars for two weeks.
One more thing: avoid personal attacks. Criticise the decision, not the politician.
I wrote that he does not care. I will take that out.
How long can the letter be?
Three thousand characters at most. Shorter texts get read more often — and shared.
We will print it on Thursday, and the municipality will get a chance to reply.
Then at least we have started a debate.
The landlord wants to raise the rent and enter without notice. A legal adviser explains what the law allows and where to complain.
The landlord announced that the rent will rise fifteen per cent from next month.
That does not sound lawful. What does your contract say?
As a general rule the rent can only be adjusted by the consumer price index once a year.
And he has to give notice in advance?
Yes, in writing and at least one month before.
He also drops in without telling me, to “check the flat”.
He is not allowed to. The home is yours while you rent it.
The fridge has been broken for three weeks. Who pays?
The landlord has a duty to maintain. You can demand repair or a reduction in rent.
Then you send a written demand with a deadline and complain to the rent disputes tribunal afterwards.
Always write by email, then you have documentation.
Thank you. Now I know both what I can demand and how.
Musa signs his daughter up for football and learns that the club runs on volunteer parents: the kiosk, driving to matches, a police certificate and community spirit.
Hi! My daughter wants to start playing football. Is there a place in the team?
Absolutely. We take everyone, whatever their level.
The training fee is a thousand a year, and the club is run by volunteers.
What is expected of the parents?
A few kiosk shifts a season and driving to away matches.
I can manage that. I work shifts, but weekends are often free.
Do I need any paperwork to help as a coach?
Yes, a police certificate. Everyone who works with children must submit one.
Why do people bother to spend so much free time on this?
Because the club is the glue in the neighbourhood. Without volunteering there would be nothing on offer.
Put me down for the kiosk in September. I will bring baklava too.
Then you will be the most popular parent of the year!
Mia and Leo go into a café. They order coffee, cocoa and a waffle, ask about the price and pay by card.
Hi! What can I help you with?
Hi! We would like a coffee and a cocoa.
And a waffle, please. With jam!
A waffle with jam and brown cheese. Anything else?
No thanks. How much is it altogether?
Yes, of course. Hold the card here.
Shall we sit by the window?
Yes, there is a free table there.
The waffle is really good. Thanks for today!
You are welcome. Next time you are paying!
to treat, to pay for someone
Leo and Nora are out in the park. They play ball, share, get used to the Norwegian weather and go home when it gets dark.
Hi, Nora! Do you want to play ball?
Yes, gladly! I will be in goal.
Oops! It went right over me.
Can I join? I have no one to play with.
Of course you can! We always share.
It is starting to rain a little.
That does not matter. We have good jackets.
Look, there are berries growing here!
We will take some home to Mum.
It is getting dark. We have to go home now.
Thanks for today! See you tomorrow!
Ruslan cannot read the road signs clearly. He goes to an optician, has his eyes tested, picks a frame and learns when the glasses will be ready.
Hello. I see the road signs badly when I drive.
Then we will do an eye test. Please sit down here.
I can only manage the third line.
Do I have to wear them all the time?
No, only when you drive and read signs.
All right. Which frame suits me?
The black one is simple and cheap — two thousand kroner.
Does my insurance cover any of it?
Ask your employer — many of them cover glasses for screen work.
Good tip! When will the glasses be ready?
Alina has found a second-hand bike in an ad. She arranges a meeting, checks it over, haggles a little and pays through an app.
Look here — a used bike for eight hundred kroner.
Alina sends a message to the seller.
Hi! Here is the bike. It is three years old.
May I try it a little?
That is right. It needs adjusting.
Could we say six hundred then?
Seven hundred, and you get the light and the lock with it.
Deal. I will pay with the app now.
Good. Let me know if anything is wrong.
Thanks! Now I will cycle to work every day.
Musa takes the bus in a new city for the first time. He buys a ticket in the app, works out the zones and the child fare — and then an inspector gets on.
I have to buy a ticket in the app before we get on.
Do I need my own ticket, Dad?
Yes, but children under six travel for free.
I am seven. Then you have to buy a child ticket.
The app asks about the zone. Which zone are we in?
He looks at the map in the app: zone 1.
Good day, ticket inspection. May I see your ticket?
Yes, here. It was activated two minutes ago.
All in order. Remember to activate before you board.
Then there is a fine — eleven hundred kroner.
Wow! Dad, always buy a ticket!
At the emergency clinic at night
Maria has a bad earache in the night. She calls 116 117, goes to the emergency clinic, explains her symptoms, waits her turn and gets a prescription.
My ear hurts and I have a fever. Is it dangerous?
She calls the emergency clinic on 116 117.
How long have you had the pain?
Since yesterday evening. It got worse during the night.
You will have to wait a little. The sickest are seen first.
I understand. Roughly how long will it be?
Let me look at the ear. Yes, it is an infection.
Yes. I will send the prescription to the pharmacy electronically.
Could I get a sick note for tomorrow?
Yes, two days. Get in touch if the fever keeps up.
Thank you so much for the help in the middle of the night.
in the middle of the night
Denys is handed a third task in a row. He learns to decline politely: he names his workload, asks the manager to choose priorities and offers an alternative.
Could you take the report too? It is a bit urgent.
I would like to help, but then we need to look at the order of things.
Right now I have the budget for Friday and the client meeting tomorrow.
Which of the three matters most to you?
Then I will do the report on Monday, or Kari could start on it.
Good solution. I will ask Kari.
Thanks for listening. I am not saying no to you, but to overtime.
Completely fair. We do not want to wear you out.
Speak up early next time as well — it makes planning easier.
Deal. A clear no is better than half a yes.
Mia and Leo measure each other, compare scarves, backpacks and dogs — and learn to describe everything around them: tall and short, long and short, big and small, heavy and light.
Look! I am tall. You are short.
No, I am not short. I am just a bit shorter than you.
Who is the tallest in the family?
Dad is the tallest, and Leo is taller than me.
Your backpack is heavy. Mine is light.
It is heavy because it is full of books.
My scarf is long. Yours is short.
Yes, but mine is thick and warm. Yours is thin.
That dog is big, and that one is small.
The small one is fast. The big one is slow.
My bike is old, but it is good.
Mine is new and fast. We are equally happy!
Musa views a flat and describes everything he sees: light or dark, clean or dirty, quiet or noisy, expensive or cheap. Along the way he learns to say politely what does not suit him.
Welcome! The flat is light and clean.
Yes, but the hallway is rather dark.
Is it quiet here in the evening?
The street is a bit noisy, but the windows are new and tight.
The storage room is empty. Is it big enough for bikes?
Two bikes fit. Three would be too tight.
The rent is twelve thousand a month.
That is expensive for me. Is there anything cheaper?
We have a smaller flat in the same house. It is older.
Old is fine if it is warm and dry.
It is both warm and cheaper. Would you like to see it?
Gladly! Small and warm is better than big and cold.
